title: Alberta Premier Tells Indian Students With Expired Visas to 'Go Home' as PGWP Crisis Deepens
excerpt: Danielle Smith's blunt message comes as over 1,500 Indian graduates face work permit denials after Portage College programs ruled ineligible by federal immigration authorities.
body:
• Alberta Premier Danielle Smith told Indian students with expired visas and no permanent residency that they "need to go home," while acknowledging some colleges may have overstated pathways to residency.
  • Over 1,500 Indian graduates in Calgary face PGWP denials after Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada ruled their non-credit programs ineligible — a clarification students say was applied retroactively.
  • Students who paid upwards of $32,000 CAD in tuition have launched hunger strikes, rallies across Alberta, and judicial reviews in Federal Court demanding the refusals be reversed.
  • Canada's broader immigration tightening aims to bring temporary residents below 5% of the total population by 2027, with PGWP eligibility narrowing and the Parents and Grandparents Program suspended for new applications.

Smith Delivers Blunt Message at Joint Presser With Carney

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith left little room for ambiguity when asked about hundreds of Indian students protesting denied work permits outside Portage College campuses in Calgary.

"Our view is that if you come here as an international student and your visa expires and you don't have permanent residency, you need to go home," Smith said at a joint press conference with Prime Minister Mark Carney.

"I think perhaps Portage, maybe overstated the pathway to permanent residency."

— Danielle Smith, Alberta Premier

Smith stopped short of calling Portage College a diploma mill but acknowledged that "unscrupulous operators have set up diploma-granting programs and taking advantage of students." She noted Alberta has only 6,400 permanent residency spots against roughly 40,000 applicants, calling for "a bit of a better balance."

Carney, speaking before Smith, said he was not familiar with the details of the Portage situation but that "there is a process to follow when such situations arise."

How 1,500 Graduates Ended Up in Limbo

The crisis traces back to a June 24, 2026 update on the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada website stating that non-credit programs — other than flight school — are not eligible for post-graduation work permits. IRCC maintains this was a clarification of existing rules, not a policy change.

But the roughly 500 graduates of Portage College and its partner institution, the Canadian Institute of Osteopathic Therapy, say the programs were listed as eligible when they enrolled in 2024. Community organizers put the total number of affected graduates in Calgary at over 1,500.

Most are from Punjab and Haryana. Many paid upwards of $32,000 CAD in tuition — around ₹19.5 lakh — on the understanding that completing the two-year diploma would lead to a three-year open work permit and a pathway to permanent residency. Instead, rejections began spiking after July 7, with some classmates from identical intakes receiving approvals while others were denied.

Hunger Strikes, Rallies, and Federal Court Challenges

A small group of students began a hunger strike on July 24 in Calgary, escalating weeks of rallies across Alberta. One student from Punjab told reporters her family had sold land to fund her move to Canada, spending ₹22–25 lakh, and that she had gone hungry for three days. Another said she missed her grandfather's funeral because of the permit limbo.

Regulated Canadian immigration consultant Dimple Verma has backed a petition calling on IRCC to halt the bulk refusals and "reverse the unpublished policy change quietly added to the IRCC website." Some graduates have already filed for judicial review in Federal Court.

"What this situation reveals is a failure of coordination between provincial and federal governments," said Matthew McDonald, a registered Canadian immigration consultant, according to The PIE News.

Portage College has distanced itself from the immigration decisions. "The college has no involvement in the review, assessment, or determination of individual immigration applications," said Jaime Davies, the college's corporate communications manager, in a July 21 statement.

Part of a Broader Immigration Tightening

The PGWP crisis unfolds against a backdrop of aggressive immigration tightening by Ottawa. Canada introduced caps on international student permits in late 2024 and has steadily narrowed PGWP eligibility through 2025 and 2026. On July 15, IRCC suspended the Parents and Grandparents Program for new applications.

The government's stated goal is to bring temporary residents below 5% of Canada's total population by 2027. In the first half of 2026 alone, Canada deported over 3,300 Indians, topping all nationalities.

Students have submitted a formal appeal to Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar seeking diplomatic intervention, according to Madhyamam Online. With the Tata Sons AGM scheduled for August 18 and broader economic uncertainty, the diplomatic ask faces an uphill climb.

What's Next

The Federal Court judicial reviews will determine whether IRCC's retroactive application of the non-credit rule violated procedural fairness. Immigration Minister Lena Diab has maintained that "non-credit programs have never qualified for these PGWP" and indicated no grandfathering is planned.

For the affected students, the options are narrowing: find a different visa pathway, retain legal counsel for court challenges, or return to India with depleted savings and no Canadian credential to show for it.
nri_angle: Over 1,500 Indian graduates in Canada, mostly from Punjab and Haryana, face deportation after post-graduation work permits were denied due to a retroactive federal rule clarification.
author: Diaspora Desk
